source.title: Scott Bessent: an economic D-Day is coming for Iran
source.author: Scott Bessent, US Secretary of the Treasury
source.note: Source text held locally and not committed — FT terms prohibit redistribution. Only short spans quoted here, for criticism.

fact.claim: Trump and the US military 'significantly dismantled Iran's military capabilities and weakened its nuclear programme'.
fact.verifyWith: IAEA verification and monitoring reports on Iran; Defense Department and DIA battle damage assessments. Note the op-ed states this without citing either.

fact.claim: 'the rial has never been weaker and inflation has rarely been higher'
fact.verifyWith: Central Bank of Iran official rate plus open-market rial quotes; Statistical Centre of Iran CPI series. Check whether 'never been weaker' is nominal or inflation-adjusted — the two give different answers.

fact.claim: The Islamic Republic has existed for 47 years.
The Allied powers convened the Tehran Conference in 1943, where Roosevelt and Churchill weighed the campaign leading to the Normandy landings.
fact.verifyWith: Standard historical record. Accurate, and doing rhetorical work — see the unity finding below.

persuasion.span: As Roosevelt and Churchill weighed a campaign that would culminate in the Normandy landings
persuasion.mechanism: Places present-day sanctions policy inside the Allied coalition of the Second World War, so that cooperating reads as joining a historically righteous alliance and declining reads as breaking from it.
persuasion.neutral: The United States is coordinating economic measures with allied governments.

persuasion.span: At dawn begins an economic D-Day
persuasion.mechanism: Sets an imminent deadline, compressing the time a government has to weigh alternatives and making deliberation itself look like hesitation.
persuasion.neutral: The sanctions programme takes effect immediately.

persuasion.span: the single greatest financial offensive ever marshalled against an adversary
persuasion.mechanism: Superlative plus military vocabulary asserts unprecedented scale as established fact, with no comparison offered against prior sanctions programmes.
persuasion.neutral: a broader sanctions programme than previous ones

persuasion.span: a malignant force in the world
persuasion.mechanism: Disease metaphor carries a moral verdict the sentence never evidences, and frames the subject as something to be excised rather than negotiated with.
persuasion.neutral: an adversary of the United States

persuasion.mechanism: Recasts sovereign states with commercial ties as accomplices, assigning them to the adversary's side before any argument about their conduct is made.
Attributes a psychological failing to states that disagree, so that disagreement reads as cowardice rather than as a different reading of their own interests.
persuasion.neutral: governments that have chosen to maintain relations with Iran

persuasion.mechanism: Borrows philosophical weight for a policy threat. Pascal's wager concerns belief under uncertainty about salvation, not compliance with sanctions; the analogy lends gravity without supplying an argument.
persuasion.neutral: Governments must weigh the risk of continued dealings with Iran.

persuasion.span: the political class accepted an endless cycle of provocation instead of advancing American interests
persuasion.mechanism: Restates decades of containment policy as passive acceptance, a position no policymaker held in those terms, which makes it easy to dismiss without engaging the actual reasoning.
persuasion.neutral: previous administrations pursued containment rather than regime collapse

persuasion.mechanism: Substitutes a threat characterisation for a threat assessment, raising perceived severity without stating likelihood or capability.
persuasion.neutral: the Iranian government's stated hostility toward the United States

persuasion.span: The alternative for those who tether themselves to Tehran is the foreclosure of any path to lasting prosperity.
persuasion.mechanism: Presents two outcomes as exhaustive — sever ties and prosper, or keep them and be ruined — excluding partial compliance, negotiated exemptions, or simply absorbing the cost.
persuasion.neutral: Countries that continue trading with Iran may face restricted access to US financial markets.

persuasion.span: Any remaining tie to Tehran will hasten the economic ostracism of countries and entities
persuasion.mechanism: Ostracism arrives as though by natural process. The US Treasury, which would decide and impose it, is absent from the sentence — so the consequence looks inevitable rather than chosen.
persuasion.neutral: The Treasury Department will sanction countries and entities that maintain ties to Tehran.

persuasion.mechanism: The collapse is presented as an ambient condition rather than the intended effect of the policy being announced in this very piece.
persuasion.neutral: where US sanctions have cut off access to legitimate finance

actionable.question: Does severing ties with Iran actually deepen a country's access to global capital, as the piece promises?
actionable.how: Compare sovereign spreads and capital inflows for states that exited Iranian trade under earlier sanctions rounds against those that didn't. The claim is empirical and checkable.

actionable.question: What specifically counts as a 'tie' that triggers secondary sanctions?
actionable.how: The op-ed names no threshold anywhere. OFAC designation notices and FAQ guidance carry the actual criteria — read those instead of the article.

actionable.question: Is the rial claim nominal or real?
actionable.how: 'Never been weaker' against a currency in high inflation is close to trivially true in nominal terms. Check the inflation-adjusted series before treating it as evidence of policy effect.

actionable.question: Who is not quoted here?
actionable.how: The piece contains no opposing voice, no cost estimate for third countries, and no named source. That is normal for an op-ed — worth noticing that it is being read alongside news coverage that looks similar on the page.

unclassified.span: are Iran's enablers willing to wager their future against it?
unclassified.note: Direct rhetorical address to the reader, closing on a question that presumes its own framing. No taxonomy category covers second-person address. Candidate for v0.2.
